cited_details.statement: HiDDeN, introduced by Zhu, Kaplan, Johnson, and Fei-Fei, is the canonical reference point: it formulates the encoder and decoder as convolutional networks, optimizes a reconstruction loss on the recovered message together with an adversarial loss for visual fidelity, and exposes the decoder to a parametric noise layer (e.g., Gaussian, JPEG, crop) during training so that the system learns to be robust against a chosen class of perturbations [HiDDeN](https://arxiv.org/abs/1807.09937).

Building on the same template, StegaStamp focuses on the print-cam capture distortion model: Tancik, Bonnet, Noorani, and Fredrikson describe a deep encoder–decoder that learns to embed hyperlink bit-strings into photographs such that they can be decoded back from re-photographed images containing lighting, perspective, and occlusion variation [StegaStamp](https://arxiv.org/abs/1904.05343).

A 2021 IEEE Access paper by Duan, Liu, and colleagues (the convolutional autoencoder for image steganography) trains an encoder/decoder pair end-to-end on datasets such as COCO, CelebA, and ImageNet and reports high PSNR with high hiding capacity, illustrating how the end-to-end paradigm scales gracefully when both inputs and outputs are dense image tensors [End-to-End Image Steganography](https://doi.org/10.1109/access.2021.3113953).

Likewise, the *Robust Spatial-spread Deep Neural Image Watermarking* work formulates watermarking as an end-to-end problem in which the message is spread across the spatial dimensions of the image and recovered by a convolutional decoder, a design that improves robustness against localized distortions [Robust Spatial-spread](https://www.semanticscholar.org/paper/b1ffb4adfc9ec647d5dee15cd3dacce1a662ffe5).

Zhong, Huang, Mastorakis, and Shih describe an "automated and robust" DNN watermarking scheme that adapts the embedding strength dynamically on a per-image basis and demonstrates multi-bit recovery under common image-processing attacks [Automated Robust DNN Watermarking](https://arxiv.org/abs/2007.02460).

Zhong and Shih's earlier 2019 work similarly couples an encoder/decoder with a differentiable approximation of common distortions to yield robustness without manual tuning [Robust DNN Watermarking](https://arxiv.org/abs/1908.11331).

On the efficiency side, Xu, Wang, Wei, and Lu propose a compact neural-network-based watermarking algorithm that preserves the end-to-end training recipe but with a markedly smaller model footprint, which is relevant for deployment on resource-constrained devices [Compact NN Watermarking](https://arxiv.org/abs/2112.13491).

Finally, the OpenReview paper "Hidden in the Noise" reports a two-stage robust watermarking scheme whose first stage is an end-to-end DNN, again demonstrating the prevalence of jointly trained encoders/decoders as the default learning framework [Hidden in the Noise](https://openreview.net/forum?id=ll2nz6qwRG).

The trained model is applied to a *distinct* test set in a bulk manner, illustrating that the network has learned a reusable image-to-feature mapping rather than a single-image lookup [General DNN Watermarking](https://arxiv.org/abs/2003.12428).
Because the network never modifies the cover image, the approach is naturally lossless and is robust to a wide range of distortions [NasNet-Mobile + DCT](https://doi.org/10.3390/electronics12163444).

The same idea has been analyzed in a comparative SSRN study of transform-domain watermarking methods versus deep-feature-based detection models, which reports that learned features can outperform hand-crafted transform-domain descriptors in detection accuracy [Transform Domain Watermarking](https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/Delivery.cfm/f8d0a745-298f-46cc-a18f-2f8d4ff89fe2-MECA.pdf?abstractid=6620161&mirid=1).

The deep component provides a learned robustness prior that the hand-crafted block-DCT scheme cannot achieve on its own [Multi-scale Auto-encoder + JPEG](https://ietresearch.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1049/ipr2.12961).

The NasNet-Mobile + DCT zero-watermarking scheme for medical images discussed above is also a clear hybrid: the deep network supplies features, the DCT supplies a stable representation, and the zero-watermarking construction logic is entirely classical [NasNet-Mobile + DCT](https://doi.org/10.3390/electronics12163444).

Likewise, the *DBMark* system by Ye, Gao, Xie, Yin, and Wei explicitly combines a deep encoder/decoder with a "deep boosting" module that draws on classical spread-spectrum intuitions; the deep side learns the residual signal that the classical part cannot model, with a reported improvement in robustness over purely learned baselines [DBMark](https://arxiv.org/abs/2210.13801).

Jia and colleagues provide another hybrid exemplar, in which *real* JPEG compression is used to harden the decoder while a *simulated* differentiable JPEG is used during joint training — the network learns a learned codec-aware embedding that is then deployed in a classical JPEG-compatible format [Enhancing Robustness via JPEG](https://dl.acm.org/doi/pdf/10.1145/3474085.3475324).

The aforementioned "Go Wide or Go Deep" study by Jia, Fang, Ma, and Zhang also straddles the paradigm boundary by treating width/depth as a per-image resource allocation problem that mixes a learned embedding with a classical allocation policy [Go Wide or Go Deep](https://arxiv.org/abs/2204.11513).

Wang, Lin, Zhao, and Zhu demonstrate that an adversary can train a "watermark faker" network that produces a forged image that fools an existing watermark detector into reporting the presence (or absence) of a watermark that was never embedded, raising the question of whether end-to-end detectors must be hardened against adversarial perturbation [Watermark Faker](https://arxiv.org/abs/2103.12489).

shows that aggressively reducing the encoder/decoder size is feasible without catastrophic loss of robustness, which is important for on-device watermarking [Compact NN Watermarking](https://arxiv.org/abs/2112.13491).

"Go Wide or Go Deep" further argues that a one-size-fits-all network is sub-optimal and that the embedding network should be selected per image, suggesting that future systems will mix a learned model zoo with a classical controller [Go Wide or Go Deep](https://arxiv.org/abs/2204.11513).

Across the three paradigms, the field has converged on a small set of recurring design patterns: an encoder/decoder pair trained end-to-end against a differentiable noise layer [HiDDeN](https://arxiv.org/abs/1807.09937), a deep feature extractor that feeds a classical transform-domain watermarking rule [NasNet-Mobile + DCT](https://doi.org/10.3390/electronics12163444), and hybrid schemes that fuse learned components with classical signal-processing primitives such as DCT and JPEG [Multi-scale Auto-encoder + JPEG](https://ietresearch.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1049/ipr2.12961), [Enhancing Robustness via JPEG](https://dl.acm.org/doi/pdf/10.1145/3474085.3475324), [DBMark](https://arxiv.org/abs/2210.13801).

evidence.title: A General Approach for Using Deep Neural Network for Digital Watermarking
evidence.abstract: Technologies of the Internet of Things (IoT) facilitate digital contents such as images being acquired in a massive way. However, consideration from the privacy or legislation perspective still demands the need for intellectual content protection. In this paper, we propose a general deep neural network (DNN) based watermarking method to fulfill this goal. Instead of training a neural network for protecting a specific image, we train on an image set and use the trained model to protect a distinct test image set in a bulk manner. Respective evaluations both from the subjective and objective aspects confirm the supremacy and practicability of our proposed method. To demonstrate the robustness of this general neural watermarking mechanism, commonly used manipulations are applied to the watermarked image to examine the corresponding extracted watermark, which still retains sufficient recognizable traits. To the best of our knowledge, we are the first to propose a general way to perform watermarking using DNN. Considering its performance and economy, it is concluded that subsequent studies that generalize our work on utilizing DNN for intellectual content protection is a promising research trend.

evidence.title: End-to-End Image Steganography Using Deep Convolutional Autoencoders
evidence.abstract: Image steganography is used to hide a secret image inside a cover image in plain sight. Traditionally, the secret data is converted into binary bits and the cover image is manipulated statistically to embed the secret binary bits. Overloading the cover image may lead to distortions and the secret information may become visible. Hence the hiding capacity of the traditional methods are limited. In this paper, a light-weight yet simple deep convolutional autoencoder architecture is proposed to embed a secret image inside a cover image as well as to extract the embedded secret image from the stego image. The proposed method is evaluated using three datasets - COCO, CelebA and ImageNet. Peak Signal-to-Noise Ratio, hiding capacity and imperceptibility results on the test set are used to measure the performance. The proposed method has been evaluated using various images including Lena, airplane, baboon and peppers and compared against other traditional image steganography methods. The experimental results have demonstrated that the proposed method has higher hiding capacity, security and robustness, and imperceptibility performances than other deep learning image steganography methods.

evidence.title: A Compact Neural Network-based Algorithm for Robust Image Watermarking
evidence.abstract: Digital image watermarking seeks to protect the digital media information from unauthorized access, where the message is embedded into the digital image and extracted from it, even some noises or distortions are applied under various data processing including lossy image compression and interactive content editing. Traditional image watermarking solutions easily suffer from robustness when specified with some prior constraints, while recent deep learning-based watermarking methods could not tackle the information loss problem well under various separate pipelines of feature encoder and decoder. In this paper, we propose a novel digital image watermarking solution with a compact neural network, named Invertible Watermarking Network (IWN). Our IWN architecture is based on a single Invertible Neural Network (INN), this bijective propagation framework enables us to effectively solve the challenge of message embedding and extraction simultaneously, by taking them as a pair of inverse problems for each other and learning a stable invertible mapping. In order to enhance the robustness of our watermarking solution, we specifically introduce a simple but effective bit message normalization module to condense the bit message to be embedded, and a noise layer is designed to simulate various practical attacks under our IWN framework. Extensive experiments demonstrate the superiority of our solution under various distortions.

evidence.title: A Robust Image Watermarking System Based on Deep Neural Networks
evidence.abstract: Digital image watermarking is the process of embedding and extracting watermark covertly on a carrier image. Incorporating deep learning networks with image watermarking has attracted increasing attention during recent years. However, existing deep learning-based watermarking systems cannot achieve robustness, blindness, and automated embedding and extraction simultaneously. In this paper, a fully automated image watermarking system based on deep neural networks is proposed to generalize the image watermarking processes. An unsupervised deep learning structure and a novel loss computation are proposed to achieve high capacity and high robustness without any prior knowledge of possible attacks. Furthermore, a challenging application of watermark extraction from camera-captured images is provided to validate the practicality as well as the robustness of the proposed system. Experimental results show the superiority performance of the proposed system as comparing against several currently available techniques.
